newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH CABINET BODY APPROVES CAR ASSEMBLY LICENCES.
newsitem.headline: POLISH CABINET BODY APPROVES CAR ASSEMBLY LICENCES.

text.p: The Polish government's economic committee approved on Monday a set of amendments to Poland's customs regulations which introduce licences for car assembly in Poland, the KERM's secretary told a news brifing.

Marek Wagner said under the new rules companies which want to assemble cars in Poland would have to meet specific capital, employment and production criteria to obtain a licence from the Economy Ministry for duty-free imports of car parts.
"We hope that the new regulations will come into force from the start of 1997," Wagner said.

He said that under the new rules a company which would want to assemble passenger cars would need to have fixed assets worth at least 10 million ECU, produce at least 8,000 cars annually and employ at least 1,000 workers.

The respective requirements for van assembly were 10 million ECU, 4,000 vans of annuall production and 600 workers while for truck assembly the threshold figures were three million Ecu, 600 trucks annually and 400 employed.
Wagner said that under the new rules companies already operating in Poland would have nine months to adjust to the new standars while newcomers, would have 12 months to meet the criteria.
The amendments have yet to be approved by the whole cabinet and clear the parliament to become binding.
Transport Minister Boguslaw Liberadzki, also present, said that the new regulations also cut the maximum age of used passenger cars to five years from the current 10 years.
The maximum age of used imported trucks would remain unchanged at three years. Liberadzki said the regulations would also practically eliminate any privately assembled cars.
"These solutions are aimed to raise the standards of cars on our roads," Liberadzki told reporters.

The government has earlier said it wanted to curb car assembly from imported kits in favour of full car production to encourage international automotive companies to invest more in Poland's booming car market.

According to an independent monitoring agency Samar, new car sales in Poland jumped nearly 40 percent in the first ten months of 1996 compared with the same period last year, showing the biggest growth rate in Europe.
During the 10 months, the number of newly registered delivery vehicles jumped by nearly 63 percent against the same period of 1995.
